outcome: The general Zarankiewicz problem remains open, but a cluster of results since November 2024 has moved specific Zarankiewicz numbers z(m,n;s,t): Davies, Gill & Horsley (arXiv 2411.18842, published Discrete Mathematics 349 (2026), art. 114924) improved upper bounds on z(m,n;s,t) via a strengthened linear program; and Bhan, Nobili & Langer (arXiv 2605.01120, May 2026) used an LLM-guided evolutionary search (OpenEvolve) to find matrix constructions that pin down three previously-unknown exact values (Z(11,21;3,3)=116, Z(11,22;3,3)=121, Z(12,22;3,3)=132), 41 new lower bounds, and 4 matched closed cases. Several further preprints (Aug-Sep 2026, by other independent authors) report additional exact-value determinations and bound improvements on z(m,n;3,3) and z(43;2) using purely classical/computational methods, with LLMs used only for writing/exploratory assistance or not at all. None of these results settle the general asymptotic conjecture z(n,n;s,t) = Θ(n^(2-1/s)); each moves specific finite instances.

ai.basis_quote: The results are obtained using OpenEvolve, an open-source evolutionary algorithm based on Large Language Models (LLMs) that iteratively improves algorithms for generating mathematical constructions by optimizing a reward signal tailored for this specific problem.
ai.disclosed_cost: Approximately $15 to $30 per m×n parameter case, per the paper's cost analysis, with each search phase completing in around 10 minutes.

counterexample.verified_how: The LLM-generated matrix constructions (candidate extremal bipartite-graph/binary-matrix constructions) were checked programmatically against the K_{s,t}-free constraint and compared to known upper bounds; exact values were confirmed when a construction's edge count matched a previously established upper bound.

summary: The classical Zarankiewicz problem — the general question of z(m,n;s,t) — remains open, and no result since 26 January 2024 resolves it or the standard asymptotic conjecture z(n,n;s,t)=Θ(n^(2-1/s)). But this is a problem whose 'entry' is really a large family of specific extremal numbers, and several of those specific instances moved in the window. The clearest and most load-bearing change is Davies, Gill & Horsley's improved linear-programming upper bounds (arXiv 2411.18842, submitted 28 Nov 2024, published in Discrete Mathematics 349 (2026) — a purely classical, non-AI result, now expert-reviewed via journal publication). Independently, Bhan, Nobili & Langer (arXiv 2605.01120, submitted 1 May 2026, revised 7 May 2026) used OpenEvolve, an LLM-guided evolutionary program-search framework, to discover binary-matrix constructions that pin down three new exact Zarankiewicz values and 41 new lower bounds; by the authors' own account the LLMs (named as Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 3.7, and — in later search phases — 'Claude Opus 4.6') proposed the constructions/generating programs, which were then verified deterministically (not by another LLM) against known upper bounds. This is coded ai_role 'generated' because the LLM produced the actual construction that appears in the result, with humans/code only checking it — not merely assisting, debugging or proofreading a human-authored construction. Status is 'progress' rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed' at the whole-record level because the overall problem is still open and no expert digestion of the May 2026 preprint has appeared; the specific closed cases it reports are best read as claimed-not-yet-digested exact values sitting inside an otherwise-open problem. A cluster of further Aug-Sep 2026 preprints (Saurabh 2608.26603, Afrasyab 2608.08154, Hou 2608.08549, Sadhu 2608.01606, Liu & Song 2609.07227) report further bound improvements or exact values on related z(m,n;3,3)/z(43;2) instances; most explicitly use classical/computational methods with no learned component, one (Afrasyab) discloses generic LLM (GPT) use for 'exploratory reasoning, implementation, verification, manuscript integration' — i.e. author-facing tooling, not a source of the mathematical content — which the rubric codes as ai_role none, and Liu & Song's paper concerns a related but distinct 'limited augmented Zarankiewicz number' tied to sums-of-squares rank of biquadratic forms rather than the classical bullet, so I treat that one as a related problem, not a case of this one.
competing_reading: One could argue the whole record should be 'open' with no_change_found, since the Wikipedia bullet is phrased as the fully general question and none of these results touches its asymptotic form. I instead read finite exact-value/bound results on z(m,n;s,t) as genuine cases of the stated problem — restrictions to specific (m,n,s,t) — which per §3.1 count as partial/progress rather than being dismissed as a different problem, so 'progress' rather than 'open' is the more defensible code. A second uncertainty: WebFetch's extraction of the arXiv 2605.01120 text gave inconsistent detail across repeated fetches (once omitting named models entirely, twice reproducing an identical three-phase model schedule including 'Claude Opus 4.6', a tier name I cannot independently confirm exists) — I report the names as given because they recurred verbatim across independent fetches, but flag that this could be a fetch-tool artifact rather than the paper's actual text.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the arXiv 2605.01120 PDF/LaTeX source (not mediated by a summarizing fetch tool) to confirm the exact model names and cost figures verbatim, and any subsequent expert commentary (e.g. a Discrete Mathematics or combinatorics-blog digestion) on whether the three new exact Zarankiewicz values have been independently verified.

judgement.doubts: The bullet asks for the extremal function in general; finitely many exact values for specific (m,n,s,t) are treated like new table entries (F3, degree–diameter) — bound-level movement, not a case settlement. Arguably they are just instances. Either way the status is progress or lower, not partial. Davies–Gill–Horsley and Bhan et al. move different entries at the same tier, so by step 4 the stronger AI role (generated) applies. The model names in the Bhan et al. record are uncertain because of fetch artifacts, but that does not change the code.
